lines.speaker: NARR
lines.text: Southern Italy. Seventy-one BC. The last morning of the slave war.

lines.speaker: YOU
lines.text: Spartacus! What are you doing? That's your horse!

lines.speaker: SPA
lines.text: If we win today, brother, I'll have a thousand Roman horses.

lines.speaker: YOU
lines.text: And if we lose?

lines.speaker: SPA
lines.text: Then I won't need one.

lines.speaker: NARR
lines.text: Across the valley, eight Roman legions are forming lines. They're led by the richest man in Rome.

lines.speaker: YOU
lines.text: Two years ago we were slaves in a gladiator school. Look at us now.

lines.speaker: SPA
lines.text: Look at them. They're afraid of us. Remember that.

lines.speaker: NARR
lines.text: You are a gladiator. You are Spartacus's closest friend. And you were there from the very first night. To see how it began, go back two years.

lines.speaker: NARR
lines.text: Capua, seventy-three BC. One of the gladiator schools in this city belongs to a man named Lentulus Batiatus.

lines.speaker: BAT
lines.text: Teeth. Shoulders. Turn around. Hm. This one is strong. Put him with the Thracian.

lines.speaker: YOU
lines.text: I'm not a slave! I was a farmer. Pirates took me off a ship!

lines.speaker: BAT
lines.text: And now you belong to me. Swear the oath, boy.

lines.speaker: DOC
lines.text: Every man here swore it. To be burned, chained, beaten, and killed by the sword. Say it!

lines.speaker: NARR
lines.text: The gladiator's oath is real. Roman writers quote it word for word.

lines.speaker: YOU
lines.text: I swear to be burned, chained, beaten, and killed by the sword.

lines.speaker: NARR
lines.text: That night, they lock you in a stone cell, smaller than a horse stall. Your cellmate is a Thracian.

lines.speaker: SPA
lines.text: First night?

lines.speaker: YOU
lines.text: Is it that obvious?

lines.speaker: SPA
lines.text: You're shaking. I'm Spartacus. I was a soldier once. Then a deserter. Then a slave.

lines.speaker: YOU
lines.text: How long have you been here?

lines.speaker: SPA
lines.text: Long enough to count the guards. Get some sleep. Tomorrow, the doctore will try to break you.

lines.speaker: CRI
lines.text: Thracian! Teaching the new puppy to bark?

lines.speaker: SPA
lines.text: Crixus. Go back to your corner.

lines.speaker: CRI
lines.text: Ha! Welcome to the house of Batiatus, puppy. Most of you don't last a season.

lines.speaker: NARR
lines.text: Your days begin at dawn. Every single day.

lines.speaker: DOC
lines.text: Wooden swords! To the post! Strike! Again! Again!

lines.speaker: DOC
lines.text: Twice the weight of a real sword! In the arena, the real one will feel like a feather!

lines.speaker: NARR
lines.text: The post was called the palus. Roman writers say recruits used weapons twice as heavy as real ones.

lines.speaker: YOU
lines.text: My arms. I can't lift them anymore.

lines.speaker: DOC
lines.text: The crowd pays to see you fight, not to see you rest! Shield up! Again!

lines.speaker: OEN
lines.text: Here. Eat. You'll need it.

lines.speaker: YOU
lines.text: What is this?

lines.speaker: OEN
lines.text: Barley and beans. Every day. They call us the barley men.

lines.speaker: NARR
lines.text: That nickname is real: hordearii. Bones from a gladiator graveyard in Ephesus show they ate mostly grains and beans.

lines.speaker: OEN
lines.text: And drink this after training. Plant ash in water.

lines.speaker: YOU
lines.text: Ugh! It's bitter!

lines.speaker: OEN
lines.text: Bitter, but it makes your bones strong. The doctors swear by it.

lines.speaker: OEN
lines.text: They want us fat, too. Fat protects you. A cut bleeds, but you keep fighting.

lines.speaker: YOU
lines.text: So they feed us like prize horses.

lines.speaker: SPA
lines.text: We are prize horses. Batiatus paid a lot for us. He doesn't want us dead. He wants us bleeding in front of a crowd.

lines.speaker: DOC
lines.text: You! New one! Curved sword, small shield. You'll fight in the Thracian style.

lines.speaker: YOU
lines.text: Like Spartacus?

lines.speaker: SPA
lines.text: Like my people. The Romans named a whole way of fighting after us.

lines.speaker: NARR
lines.text: Back then, the three main styles were named after peoples Rome had beaten: the Samnite, the Gaul, and the Thracian.

lines.speaker: CRI
lines.text: And I'm the Gaul. Big shield, straight sword. When we meet in the arena, puppy, try not to cry.

lines.speaker: NARR
lines.text: Three months later. Your first games.

lines.speaker: HER
lines.text: People of Capua! The house of Batiatus presents ten pairs of gladiators!

lines.speaker: OEN
lines.text: First the parade. Animal hunts in the morning. Criminals at noon. We fight in the afternoon.

lines.speaker: YOU
lines.text: There are thousands of them. Women. Children. Old men eating bread.

lines.speaker: SPA
lines.text: They're not here for you. They're here for a good fight. Give them one, and you live.

lines.speaker: NARR
lines.text: First, a warm-up with blunt weapons. Then the real swords come out.

lines.speaker: REF
lines.text: Gladiators! Fight clean. When I raise my stick, you stop. Begin!

lines.speaker: NARR
lines.text: Yes, there was a referee. Roman mosaics show him with a long stick, right between the fighters.

lines.speaker: OPP
lines.text: Come on, Thracian! Show me that little sword!

lines.speaker: YOU
lines.text: Shield up. Watch his feet. Watch his feet.

lines.speaker: SPA
lines.text: His shield covers everything! Go low! Go for the legs!

lines.speaker: OPP
lines.text: Agh! My leg!

lines.speaker: HER
lines.text: He is down! He is down!

lines.speaker: REF
lines.text: Stop! He raises a finger! He asks for mercy! The editor decides!

lines.speaker: NARR
lines.text: The editor was the rich man who paid for the games. The loser's life was in his hands.

lines.speaker: YOU
lines.text: Do I have to kill him?

lines.speaker: SPA
lines.text: Look at the crowd. Watch the editor's hand.

lines.speaker: NARR
lines.text: Movies show a thumb pointing down for death. That idea comes from a painting made in eighteen seventy-two. Nobody knows exactly what the Roman gesture looked like.

lines.speaker: HER
lines.text: The editor grants mercy! Missio!

lines.speaker: YOU
lines.text: He lives. I live.

lines.speaker: NARR
lines.text: Most fights did not end in death. Gladiators were expensive. Records from a century later suggest about one fight in five ended with a dead man.

lines.speaker: SPA
lines.text: One in five, brother. Fight ten times, and do the math.

lines.speaker: YOU
lines.text: That's not a life. That's a slow execution.

lines.speaker: SPA
lines.text: Exactly. So let's not stay.

lines.speaker: NARR
lines.text: Summer, seventy-three BC. Two hundred gladiators are planning an escape.

lines.speaker: SPA
lines.text: Tonight. The kitchen. Knives, cleavers, roasting spits. Anything with an edge.

lines.speaker: CRI
lines.text: Kitchen knives against Roman swords? You're mad, Thracian.

lines.speaker: SPA
lines.text: You have a better plan, Gaul? Or do you want to die for Batiatus's money?

lines.speaker: CRI
lines.text: Hm. I'm in.

lines.speaker: NARR
lines.text: But someone talks. The guards find out.

lines.speaker: YOU
lines.text: They know! Spartacus, they know!

lines.speaker: SPA
lines.text: Then it's now or never! Go! Go!

lines.speaker: NARR
lines.text: Of two hundred, only about seventy make it out, armed with kitchen tools.

lines.speaker: OEN
lines.text: Look! On the road! A wagon!

lines.speaker: YOU
lines.text: It's full of gladiator weapons! Real swords!

lines.speaker: SPA
lines.text: Throw away the kitchen knives, brothers. We're gladiators again. But this time, we fight for ourselves.

lines.speaker: NARR
lines.text: They hide on a mountain near Naples. You know it today as Vesuvius. In seventy-three BC, it's just a quiet, green mountain.

lines.speaker: GLA
lines.text: Three thousand men. One road up. We don't attack. We wait until they starve.

lines.speaker: NARR
lines.text: The praetor Claudius Glaber blocks the only path. Behind the rebels, there are only cliffs.

lines.speaker: WIFE
lines.text: Spartacus. I dreamed of you. A snake was coiled around your face while you slept.

lines.speaker: SPA
lines.text: Is that good, or bad?

lines.speaker: WIFE
lines.text: Both. Great power. And a terrible end.

lines.speaker: NARR
lines.text: Plutarch really tells this story. Spartacus's wife was a Thracian prophetess.

lines.speaker: YOU
lines.text: These wild vines. Look how thick they are. Spartacus, we could make ladders!

lines.speaker: SPA
lines.text: Ladders. Down the cliff. Brother, you're a genius.

lines.speaker: NARR
lines.text: That night they weave ladders from wild grapevines, and climb down the cliffs in the dark.

lines.speaker: GLA
lines.text: What's that noise? Who's out there?

lines.speaker: SPA
lines.text: Now! Attack!

lines.speaker: YOU
lines.text: They're running! Take their swords! Take their armor!

lines.speaker: NARR
lines.text: Attacked from behind, the Romans flee. The slaves take their weapons, and their whole camp.

lines.speaker: NARR
lines.text: Word spreads. Slaves run away from farms and villas all over southern Italy.

lines.speaker: YOU
lines.text: Spartacus, look! There are hundreds more on the road. Women. Old men. Children.

lines.speaker: SPA
lines.text: Let them come. Every one of them was chained, like us.

lines.speaker: OEN
lines.text: We need iron. Swords, armor, horses.

lines.speaker: SPA
lines.text: Then we take iron. But no gold. No silver. Gold makes men lazy.

lines.speaker: NARR
lines.text: Appian writes that Spartacus banned merchants from bringing gold or silver into the camp, and shared the loot equally.

lines.speaker: NARR
lines.text: Not everyone lived to see what came next. Oenomaus, who gave you his bowl on your first day, was killed in the first year.

lines.speaker: NARR
lines.text: But the army keeps growing. Seventy thousand people, led by gladiators. They beat one Roman army after another.

lines.speaker: YOU
lines.text: We beat them again! Two praetors! Two consuls!

lines.speaker: SPA
lines.text: And every time we win, they send a bigger army.

lines.speaker: NARR
lines.text: Seventy-two BC. The leaders argue about what to do next.

lines.speaker: SPA
lines.text: We go north. Over the Alps. Then everyone goes home. Thrace. Gaul. Free.

lines.speaker: CRI
lines.text: Home? Why run? Rome is weak! We should burn every villa from here to the sea!

lines.speaker: SPA
lines.text: And then what? Rome never runs out of soldiers, Crixus. We do.

lines.speaker: CRI
lines.text: Then I'll take my Gauls and do it myself.

lines.speaker: YOU
lines.text: Crixus, don't. Together we're seventy thousand. Apart, we're two easy targets.

lines.speaker: CRI
lines.text: You're his dog, puppy. You always were. Come with me, and be a wolf.

lines.speaker: NARR
lines.text: So, who do you follow? Your best friend, or the man who wants revenge?

lines.speaker: YOU
lines.text: I stay with Spartacus.

lines.speaker: CRI
lines.text: Then good luck. Both of you.

lines.speaker: NARR
lines.text: Crixus left with about thirty thousand men. Near Mount Garganus, a consul caught them. Crixus and two thirds of his men were killed.

lines.speaker: YOU
lines.text: He's dead. Crixus is dead.

lines.speaker: SPA
lines.text: Then Rome will pay for him. The way they made us pay.

lines.speaker: NARR
lines.text: Appian writes that Spartacus held funeral games for Crixus. Three hundred Roman prisoners were forced to fight each other, like gladiators.

lines.speaker: YOU
lines.text: Now they know what it feels like.

lines.speaker: SPA
lines.text: Now they know.

lines.speaker: NARR
lines.text: Rome is terrified. The richest man in the city, Marcus Licinius Crassus, takes command.

lines.speaker: CRA
lines.text: Some of my men ran away from slaves. Line them up. Every tenth man dies.

lines.speaker: NARR
lines.text: This was called decimation. Plutarch says fifty soldiers were killed by their own comrades.

lines.speaker: YOU
lines.text: His soldiers are more afraid of him than of us now.

lines.speaker: NARR
lines.text: Spartacus heads for the sea. He wants to cross to Sicily, where thousands of slaves could join him.

lines.speaker: PIR
lines.text: Pay us, and our ships will carry your army across. You have my word.

lines.speaker: SPA
lines.text: Then we have a deal.

lines.speaker: NARR
lines.text: The pirates take the money, and sail away. They never come back.

lines.speaker: YOU
lines.text: They're gone! The ships are gone!

lines.speaker: CRA
lines.text: Dig. A ditch from sea to sea, and a wall behind it. Let them starve.

lines.speaker: NARR
lines.text: Crassus cut off the whole toe of Italy. Plutarch says the ditch was about fifty-five kilometers long.

lines.speaker: YOU
lines.text: He's trapped us. Sea on three sides, a wall on the fourth.

lines.speaker: SPA
lines.text: Then we wait for the right night.

lines.speaker: NARR
lines.text: On a snowy winter night, the rebels fill part of the ditch with earth and branches, and break through.

lines.speaker: YOU
lines.text: We're out! We're through the wall!

lines.speaker: NARR
lines.text: Spring, seventy-one BC. And now you're back on that last morning.

lines.speaker: YOU
lines.text: Spartacus. If this is the end, thank you. For the night in the kitchen. For all of it.

lines.speaker: SPA
lines.text: Don't thank me, brother. You were free before you met me. They just forgot to tell you.

lines.speaker: SPA
lines.text: Today, I want Crassus. Only Crassus.

lines.speaker: NARR
lines.text: Plutarch writes that Spartacus fought his way toward Crassus himself. He killed two centurions. He never reached him.

lines.speaker: YOU
lines.text: Spartacus! Where are you? Spartacus!

lines.speaker: NARR
lines.text: He was surrounded and cut down. His body was never found.

lines.speaker: NARR
lines.text: Six thousand captured rebels were crucified along the Appian Way, the road from Capua to Rome. For about two hundred kilometers, the crosses lined the road.

lines.speaker: YOU
lines.text: I run into the mountains. A few of us made it. Most of us didn't.

lines.speaker: NARR
lines.text: Pompey caught five thousand more running north, and told Rome he had ended the war. Crassus never forgave him.

lines.speaker: NARR
lines.text: So, how much of this is true?

lines.speaker: NARR
lines.text: Almost everything we know comes from two Greek writers, Plutarch and Appian. They wrote more than a century and a half later.

lines.speaker: YOU
lines.text: So nobody who was there wrote it down?

lines.speaker: NARR
lines.text: Nothing that survived. But in Pompeii, archaeologists found a painted fight on a wall. Above one rider, someone wrote a name: Spartaks.

lines.speaker: YOU
lines.text: Spartaks. Painted while people still remembered him?

lines.speaker: NARR
lines.text: Maybe. It's written in Oscan, an old language of the region, and the painting may be from his own lifetime.

lines.speaker: NARR
lines.text: And the famous scene where every slave stands up and shouts, I'm Spartacus? That's from a movie made in nineteen sixty. It never happened.

lines.speaker: YOU
lines.text: Two years. A stone cell, a kitchen knife, and a ladder made of vines. And the most powerful city on Earth was afraid of us.

lines.speaker: NARR
lines.text: So, if you'd been there in seventy-two BC, would you have followed Spartacus north, or Crixus into the fight? Tell me in the comments.
